claims.text: The initial TiVNbTa alloy is dendritic and has a single-phase BCC structure.
The initial TiVNbTa alloy is produced by vacuum arc melting followed by high-temperature homogenization around 1300 °C.
The baseline TiVNbTa alloy has a lower-temperature yield strength of approximately 800 MPa.
At 1273 K, the baseline TiVNbTa alloy has approximately 330 MPa yield strength.
At 1273 K and 30% strain, the baseline TiVNbTa alloy has approximately 423 MPa compressive strength.
Introducing oxygen during processing can trigger TiO precipitation within a BCC refractory-alloy matrix.
Controlled oxygen addition or annealing in a slightly oxygenated atmosphere will produce a homogeneous dispersion of fine TiO nanoparticles in TiVNbTa.
The TiO precipitates will remain thermally stable at temperatures up to 1273 K.
Fine TiO particles provide precipitation strengthening in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Nanoscale TiO particles will pin dislocations in TiVNbTa at high temperature.
Nanoscale TiO particles will inhibit grain-boundary sliding in TiVNbTa at high temperature.
The TiO dispersion will reduce thermally activated plasticity and mitigate high-temperature strength loss.
The oxygen-modified TiVNbTa alloy will retain at least about 500 MPa yield strength at 1273 K, compared with the stated 330 MPa baseline.
The oxygen-modified alloy will maintain acceptable ductility for use as an intermediate layer.
Excessive oxygen may produce brittle phases rather than a strengthening TiO dispersion.
A matched inert-processed control and oxygen-treated TiVNbTa group tested at 1273 K under identical loading rates can determine whether oxygen treatment improves high-temperature strength.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant yield-strength increase of at least about 20% relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
Formation of deleterious brittle phases instead of a fine TiO dispersion would falsify the proposed microstructural mechanism.
